items.foco: Migratory pain to the right iliac fossa
items.title: Migratory pain in appendicitis
items.contentHtml:
Migratory pain to the right iliac fossa

  • Initial visceral pain in the epigastrium or mesogastrium due to distension of the appendix (visceral afferent fibers T8-T10), then somatic pain in the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum is irritated.
  • The migration occurs in 50-60% of cases; its absence does not rule out appendicitis.
  • Differential diagnosis: Meckel's diverticulitis, mesenteric adenitis, Crohn's disease ileocecal, intussusception in children, and in women: ectopic pregnancy, torsion

items.title: Blumberg sign
items.contentHtml:
Blumberg's sign

  • It consists of pain on decompression (sudden release) at McBurney's point; indicates local peritoneal irritation.
  • It is positive in acute appendicitis when there is involvement of the parietal peritoneum, but also in other peritonitis.
  • The Rovsing sign (pain in the right iliac fossa when palpating the left iliac fossa) and the psoas sign (pain when extending the right thigh) are additional irritation maneuvers.
  • Trap: the sign may be negative in retrocecal or pelvic appendicitis; In these cases the pain on palpation may be more diffuse.

items.title: Alvarado Scale
items.contentHtml:
Alvarado Scale (MANTRELS)

  • Criteria (score): Pain migration to right iliac fossa (1), Anorexia (1), Nausea/vomiting (1), Tenderness in right iliac fossa (2), Rebound (1), Thermal elevation >37.3°C (1), Leukocytosis >10,000/mm³ (2), Left shift (neutrophils >75%) (1).
  • Interpretation: <4 low probability; 5-6 doubtful, observe; 7-8 probable appendicitis, consider surgery; 9-10 very likely, surgery.
  • In women of childbearing age, the scale has less specificity; ultrasound or computed tomography is recommended if there is doubt.

items.title: Pneumoperitoneum in perforation
items.contentHtml:
Pneumoperitoneum under the diaphragm

  • Radiological sign: subdiaphragmatic free air in standing chest x-ray or lateral decubitus; also visible on computed tomography (higher sensitivity).
  • Present in ~50-70% of hollow viscus perforations (peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, cancer).
  • The absence of pneumoperitoneum does not exclude perforation, especially if it is retroperitoneal or covered.
  • Trap: open air may be due to recent surgery (up to 7 days), pneumothorax, or peritoneal dialysis; correlate with clinical.

items.title: Volvulus vs invagination
items.contentHtml:
Intestinal obstruction: volvulus vs intussusception

  • Sigmoid volvulus: more common in the elderly, chronic constipation; symptoms of obstruction + marked distention; x-ray shows ‘coffee bean’; initial treatment with endoscopic decompression (risk of recurrence).
  • Cecal volvulus: less common, acute presentation, pain in the right lower quadrant, image in 'kidney' or 'coffee bean' in the right hemiabdomen.
  • Intestinal intussusception: typical in infants 3 months-3 years, intermittent colic pain, stools in ‘currant jelly’ (blood + mucus), palpable mass in the right hemiabdomen; ultrasound in 'target' or 'pseudo-kidney'.
  • Treatment of intussusception: barium or air enema (if there is no perforation/peritonitis); if failed or complicated, surgery.

items.foco: Intermittent cramping pain with abdominal distention
items.title: Obstructive cramping pain
items.contentHtml:
Intermittent colicky pain with distention

  • Typical pattern of mechanical intestinal obstruction: colicky (periumbilical) pain in waves, associated with abdominal distension, vomiting and absence of evacuation/gas.
  • The pain is intermittent because peristalsis increases against the obstruction; if it becomes continuous, suspect ischemia or strangulation.
  • Causes: postoperative adhesions (more common), hernias, neoplasms, volvulus, invagination.
  • Plain x-ray: air-fluid levels in a ladder; CT scan confirms level and cause.

items.title: Peritonitis: contracture and rebound
items.contentHtml:
Peritonitis: abdominal contracture and rebound

  • Cardinal signs: abdominal contracture (involuntary rigidity) and rebound (pain on decompression); indicate diffuse peritoneal irritation.
  • The contracture is involuntary (does not subside with relaxation) and reflects muscle spasm due to peritoneal inflammation.
  • It may be accompanied by fever, tachycardia, ileus and generalized abdominal pain.
  • Causes: perforation of the hollow viscus, complicated appendicitis, diverticulitis, necrotizing pancreatitis, postoperative.
  • Management: fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics (covering gram-negative and anaerobes, e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours) and laparotomy urgent .

items.foco: Mesenteric ischemia: pain disproportionate to the examination
items.title: Mesenteric ischemia
items.contentHtml:
Acute mesenteric ischemia

  • Key: severe abdominal pain of sudden onset, disproportionate to the findings of the physical examination (soft abdomen at the beginning).
  • Risk factors: atrial fibrillation (embolism), atherosclerosis (thrombosis), hypoperfusion (not occlusive), hypercoagulability.
  • Diagnosis: computed tomography angiography (non-invasive gold standard); laboratory: elevated lactate (late), leukocytosis.
  • Management: resuscitation, antibiotics, and revascularization (embolectomy/bypass) or intestinal resection if there is necrosis.
  • Trap: absence of peritoneal signs does not rule out; Delay increases mortality.

items.title: Murphy's sign
items.contentHtml:
Acute cholecystitis: Murphy's sign

  • Murphy's sign: interruption of deep inspiration due to pain on palpation in the right hypochondrium (inflamed gallbladder).
  • The ultrasound Murphy's sign (pain when passing the transducer over the gallbladder) has high specificity (~90%) for cholecystitis. acute.
  • Tokyo criteria (2018): local inflammation (pain, Murphy, mass), systemic inflammation (fever, elevated CRP, leukocytosis), and imaging evidence (wall thickening >4 mm, perivesicular fluid).
  • Management: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 hours) + antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone 1 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV).

items.foco: Acute pancreatitis: elevated amylase and lipase
items.title: Acute pancreatitis: enzymes
items.contentHtml:
Acute pancreatitis: amylase and lipase

  • Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: typical abdominal pain (epigastric radiating to the back), lipase or amylase >3 times the upper limit of normal, or compatible image.
  • Lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase; it rises earlier and persists longer.
  • Amylase may be normal in chronic alcoholic pancreatitis or hypertriglyceridemia; It is also elevated in parotitis, intestinal obstruction, and bile duct disease.
  • Evaluate severity: Ranson criteria (on admission and at 48 hours), APACHE-II, CRP, and hematocrit; computed tomography with contrast if there is doubt or after 72 hours for necrosis.

items.foco: Diverticulitis: pain in the left iliac fossa
items.title: Acute diverticulitis
items.contentHtml:
Acute diverticulitis

  • Classic presentation: pain in left iliac fossa (FII), fever, change in bowel habit, nausea.
  • In Caucasians, the sigmoid colon is the most affected (~90%); in Asians it can be right.
  • Diagnosis: computed tomography with contrast (gold standard), shows wall thickening, diverticula, inflammation of the pericolonic fat; Hinchey classification (I-IV).
  • Management: uncomplicated (Hinchey I) can be treated on an outpatient basis with oral antibiotics (e.g. ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours + metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours) or liquid diet; Complicated (abscess, perforation) requires hospitalization and possible drainage/surgery.

items.foco: Strangulated hernia: irreducible with inflammatory signs
items.title: strangulated hernia
items.contentHtml:
Strangulated hernia

  • Definition: irreducible hernia with vascular compromise of the contents (intestinal loop or other), which produces ischemia and necrosis if not treated.
  • Alarm signs: intense pain, erythema of the skin, fever, tachycardia, intestinal obstruction, and peritoneal signs.
  • Irreducibility does not always equate to strangulation; the latter is a surgical emergency.
  • Management: resuscitation with fluids, antibiotics (cover gram-negative and anaerobes), and urgent surgery (hernioplasty + intestinal resection if necessary).
  • Trap: do not attempt forced manual reduction in case of strangulation; riesgo de perforación.
